$data_availability_finding: waist_cm is absent from BOTH BRFSS (all 330 columns checked) and DiaBD.
Only NHANES carries it. family_history is absent from BRFSS entirely and
broken in DiaBD (3.2% prevalence, univariate AUC 0.492).
So NHANES is the primary training source despite being the smallest,
because it is the only one with waist, a working family history, and
lab-confirmed labels. BRFSS supplies breadth on the features it does have.

1.name: Screening
1.description: Questionnaire + anthropometry only. What most users get.

2.name: High confidence
2.description: Adds user-entered lab values. Narrower estimate.

features.name: age_years
features.notes: Hard block below 18 (PRD 3.3). BRFSS ships 5-year bands, not integers; decode to band midpoints and record that the training age is coarser than the runtime age.

features.name: sex_at_birth
features.notes: Needed for BMR, waist cutoffs, and the gestational-diabetes branch. Distinct from gender identity; the UI must say 'sex at birth' and explain why.

features.name: height_cm
features.notes: Collected to derive BMI and waist-to-height ratio. Not a model input on its own.

features.name: waist_cm
features.notes: CRITICAL for South Asians (PRD 7.1) and an IDRS input. BRFSS 2015 has no waist variable, so the pretraining corpus cannot supply it — the model must handle waist as missing-at-pretrain and present-at-finetune. LightGBM handles missing natively; do NOT impute it.

features.name: family_history
features.notes: Strongest non-modifiable factor and the hook for the Family tier (PRD F11). DiaBD is binary; map to none/first_degree and record the information loss.

features.name: physical_activity
features.notes: IDRS input. BRFSS only distinguishes any/none — a 5-level runtime scale trained on a 2-level source is a real mismatch; collapse at training time, not at runtime.

features.name: gestational_diabetes_history
features.notes: ADA Risk Test input. Null for male profiles — null means not-applicable here, not unknown.

features.name: known_high_bp
features.notes: LEAKAGE SUSPECT (Playbook B2). Hypertension is frequently diagnosed at the same visit as the diabetes, so in BRFSS it partly encodes 'has seen a doctor recently' rather than physiology — and our target user has never seen a doctor. Note it is nonetheless a legitimate FINDRISC/ADA input, so it may survive in the clinical-score layer even if the audit drops it from the GBM. Decide with the with/without AUC delta.

features.name: on_bp_meds
features.notes: LEAKAGE SUSPECT for the same reason as known_high_bp, and more strongly — being medicated requires a prescription, which requires a doctor. FINDRISC input.

features.name: history_high_glucose
features.notes: STRONGEST LEAKAGE SUSPECT. 'Have you ever been told you have high blood sugar' is close to the label itself for anyone in the healthcare system, and is unanswerable for someone who has never been tested. Expect a large AUC drop when removed — that drop is the point, not a reason to keep it. Carries a 5-point FINDRISC weight, the largest single item there.

features.name: fasting_glucose_mmol_l
features.notes: NEVER mean-impute (Playbook B7). Absence routes to Tier 1; it does not get a fabricated average. Triggers the red-flag interceptor above 13.9 or below 3.9 (PRD 3.3).

features.name: hba1c_percent
features.notes: NHANES GHB_J has 6,401 rows; the fasting subsample is only 3,036. HbA1c is the wider objective label and should anchor the Tier-2 target.

derived.name: bmi
derived.notes: Thresholds are REGIONAL, not global — see packs/*.json. Asian-Pacific uses 23/27.5, not 25/30.

derived.name: waist_to_height_ratio
derived.notes: ⭐ Playbook B9 calls this the highest-leverage single feature. Travels across ethnicities far better than BMI and is trivially measurable at home. Healthy threshold ~0.5 universally. Expect it near the top of the SHAP ranking; if it is not, suspect a bug in the waist pipeline.

excluded_for_leakage.$comment: Present in BRFSS, deliberately NOT collected and NOT trained on. Each is a consequence of diabetes or of being inside the healthcare system, and our target user is outside it (Playbook B2).
excluded_for_leakage.CholCheck: Having had a cholesterol check means you see doctors.
excluded_for_leakage.HighChol: Frequently diagnosed at the same visit as the diabetes.
excluded_for_leakage.GenHlth: Self-rated health — heavily coloured by knowing your diagnosis.
excluded_for_leakage.MentHlth: Downstream effect; also invites a fairness problem.

label.name: has_diabetes_or_prediabetes
$comment: SCREENING, not prediction (Playbook B1). The question is 'do you already
have undiagnosed high blood sugar right now', which cross-sectional data
can actually answer. A 10-year incidence claim needs longitudinal outcome
data we do not have, and marketing one trained on cross-sectional data is
both wrong and a regulatory claim we cannot defend.

sanity_bounds.$comment: If a trained model lands outside these, stop and hunt the bug. Do not ship, and do not celebrate.
